title: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies

slides.title: The Council of the EU: the facts
slides.text: Representatives of the member states at MINISTERIAL level, meeting in sub-formations by topic — ECOFIN, COMPET, FAC, ENV, AGRIFISH and others. The presidency rotates, organised in trios. Meetings are prepared by the Committee of Permanent Representatives, Coreper I and II, and by working groups, with a Secretariat General behind them. Seat in Brussels. Note the consequence of the ministerial composition: which minister attends depends on the subject, so the 'Council' in a legal basis is always the same institution wearing a different hat.

cards.q: Who sits in the Council of the EU, and why does its composition change?
cards.a: Representatives of the member states at ministerial level. It is one single institution but meets in topic-based configurations, so the responsible national minister attends — the environment minister for ENV, the finance minister for ECOFIN.

slides.title: The rotating presidency
slides.text: A member state holds the presidency for six months and chairs the Council's meetings. It gives some scope to push nationally important issues, but the more important role is facilitating decision-making — the presidency is a broker, not a principal. Presidencies work in trios to give continuity: the 2025/26 trio is Poland (January-June 2025), Denmark (July-December 2025) and Cyprus (January-June 2026).

terms.def: Three successive presidencies coordinating an eighteen-month programme.

cards.q: What is the rotating Council presidency for, and what is a trio?
cards.a: A member state chairs the Council for six months, mainly to facilitate decision-making rather than to push its own agenda. Three consecutive presidencies form a trio coordinating an eighteen-month programme.

slides.title: The ten configurations
slides.text: One single entity meeting in ten configurations: General Affairs; Foreign Affairs, chaired by the High Representative rather than the rotating presidency; ECOFIN; Justice and Home Affairs; Agriculture and Fisheries; Employment, Social Policy, Health and Consumer Affairs; Competitiveness; Transport, Telecommunications and Energy; Environment; and Education, Youth, Culture and Sport. Beside them sits the Euro Group — the ministers of the euro-area states, existing since 2004 with an elected President (currently Paschal Donohoe) and anchored in the Lisbon Treaty.

terms.def: Informal-turned-anchored body of euro-area finance ministers with its own elected President.

cards.q: Which Council configuration is not chaired by the rotating presidency, and by whom instead?
cards.a: The Foreign Affairs Council, chaired by the High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.

slides.title: Coreper and the A/B points
slides.text: The Council's real working machinery. Coreper, the Committee of Permanent Representatives, meets in two formations: Coreper I, the deputies, handles the more technical files; Coreper II, the ambassadors, the politically sensitive ones. It sorts the agenda into two kinds of item — A points, adopted in the Council without further discussion because agreement was reached below, and B points, actually debated by the ministers. Roughly 250 working groups of civil servants feed into this. The practical lesson: most EU legislation is settled before any minister sees it.

terms.def: Committee of Permanent Representatives preparing Council meetings; I = deputies, II = ambassadors.
A points are adopted without discussion because agreement was reached in Coreper; B points are debated by ministers.

cards.q: What is the difference between an A point and a B point on a Council agenda?
cards.a: An A point is adopted without further discussion because agreement was already reached in Coreper; a B point is actually debated by the ministers.

slides.title: Article 16 TEU
slides.text: The Council shall, JOINTLY WITH THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT, exercise legislative and budgetary functions, and shall carry out policy-making and coordinating functions as laid down in the Treaties. Set this beside Article 15 on the European Council — 'shall not exercise legislative functions' — and the division is clear: the European Council directs, the Council legislates with Parliament.

cards.q: Which body legislates with the European Parliament, and which one expressly does not legislate at all?
cards.a: The Council of the EU legislates jointly with Parliament (Art 16 TEU). The European Council exercises no legislative functions (Art 15 TEU).

slides.title: Four functions
slides.text: Legislation, execution, budget, politics — the Council's four roles in one line.

slides.title: Decision-making: the overview
slides.text: Presence quorum: a simple majority of voting members. Decision-making: qualified majority as the standard, with simple majority, super-qualified majority and unanimity as the other thresholds. The next slide gives the figures, which the exam does ask for.

slides.title: The four voting thresholds
slides.text: Learn these numbers. QUALIFIED MAJORITY is the standard, used for example in the ordinary legislative procedure: 55 per cent of the member states — 15 of 27 — representing 65 per cent of the EU population (Article 16(3) and (4) TEU). It is a double majority: states AND people. SIMPLE MAJORITY, for procedural matters: 50 per cent of member states plus one (Article 238(1) TFEU). SUPER-QUALIFIED MAJORITY under Article 238(2) TFEU: 72 per cent of member states representing 65 per cent of the population — used where the Council acts without a Commission proposal. And UNANIMITY, for example in the common foreign and security policy (Article 31(1) TEU).

terms.def: 55% of member states (15 of 27) representing 65% of the Union's population — a double majority of states and people.

cards.q: State the qualified majority threshold in the Council, with the Treaty basis.
cards.a: 55 per cent of the member states — 15 of 27 — representing at least 65 per cent of the population of the Union (Art 16(3), (4) TEU). A double majority of states and of people.

cards.q: When does the Council need a super-qualified majority, and what is it?
cards.a: Under Article 238(2) TFEU, where it acts without a Commission proposal: 72 per cent of the member states representing 65 per cent of the population.

cards.q: Which voting rule applies to the common foreign and security policy?
cards.a: Unanimity (Art 31(1) TEU) — the most sovereignty-sensitive field keeps the veto.

slides.title: Three special mechanisms
slides.text: The EMERGENCY BRAKE: a member state can suspend a file and refer it to the European Council, in social security (Article 48(2) TFEU) and in criminal law (Articles 82(3) and 83(2) TFEU) — a political safety valve for qualified majority voting. REVERSE QUALIFIED MAJORITY, used in the excessive deficit procedure (Article 126 TFEU): the Commission's proposal stands UNLESS a qualified majority votes against it, which inverts the burden and strengthens the Commission enormously. And PASSERELLE CLAUSES (Articles 48(7) and 31(3) TEU), which allow a shift from unanimity to qualified majority voting without amending the Treaties.

terms.def: A member state's right to suspend a file and refer it to the European Council in defined sensitive fields.
The proposal is deemed adopted unless a qualified majority opposes it.
A Treaty provision allowing a move from unanimity to QMV without treaty amendment.

cards.q: What does a reverse qualified majority do, and where is it used?
cards.a: It inverts the burden: the Commission's proposal is adopted unless a qualified majority votes against it. Used for instance in the excessive deficit procedure under Article 126 TFEU.

cards.q: How can the Union move a field from unanimity to qualified majority voting without amending the Treaties?
cards.a: Through a passerelle clause, e.g. Article 48(7) TEU or Article 31(3) TEU — the Treaties themselves authorise the switch.

slides.title: The Parliament: the facts
slides.text: Five-year terms, directly elected since 1979, most recently in June 2024. Seats are allocated by DEGRESSIVE PROPORTIONALITY — smaller states get more seats per inhabitant than larger ones, so a Maltese MEP represents far fewer people than a German one. Formally seated in Strasbourg, with work also in Brussels and Luxembourg — the three-seat arrangement that is fixed in the Treaties and cannot be changed without unanimity.

terms.def: Seat allocation giving smaller member states more seats per inhabitant than larger ones.

cards.q: What does degressive proportionality mean for the composition of the European Parliament?
cards.a: Seats are not allocated in strict proportion to population: smaller member states receive more seats per inhabitant than larger ones, so votes are not of equal weight across the Union.

slides.title: The Parliament's composition
slides.text: A seat distribution chart from Politico showing the political groups after the 2024 election.

slides.title: The President of the Parliament
slides.text: Elected for two and a half years — half a legislative period — and re-electable; Roberta Metsola (Malta, EPP) was re-elected. The President represents Parliament externally and towards the other institutions, is responsible for applying its rules of procedure and therefore chairs all its work, and belongs to Parliament's administration alongside the Bureau, the Conference of Presidents and a Secretariat of more than 5,000 staff.

slides.title: Political groups
slides.text: MEPs sit by POLITICAL direction, not by nationality, and are seated in the chamber from left to right accordingly. A group needs 23 members drawn from at least seven member states, and nobody may belong to two groups. Each group organises itself with a chair, a board and a secretariat, and decides its position by internal discussion — but the slide ends with the point that matters constitutionally: there is NO GROUP DISCIPLINE, members cannot be compelled to vote a particular way.

cards.q: What are the formal requirements for a political group in the European Parliament?
cards.a: At least 23 members from at least seven member states, and no dual membership. Groups form by political direction rather than nationality, and there is no binding group discipline.

slides.title: Article 14 TEU
slides.text: The European Parliament shall, jointly with the Council, exercise legislative and budgetary functions; shall exercise functions of political control and consultation; and SHALL ELECT THE PRESIDENT OF THE COMMISSION. Three functions, and the third is the one that gives the institution its leverage over the executive.

cards.q: What three functions does Article 14 TEU give the European Parliament?
cards.a: Legislative and budgetary functions jointly with the Council; political control and consultation; and the election of the President of the Commission.

slides.title: Three roles
slides.text: Legislation, supervision, budget.

slides.title: How Parliament decides
slides.text: Presence quorum: one third of the members. Regular decision-making quorum: 50 per cent plus one — a majority of the votes cast. Note the asymmetry with the Council, where the presence quorum is a simple majority: Parliament can act with far fewer members in the room, which is why headline votes are whipped even without formal group discipline.

cards.q: What are the presence and decision quorums in the European Parliament?
cards.a: Presence quorum one third of members; regular decisions by 50 per cent plus one of the votes cast.

slides.title: The European Central Bank
slides.text: Independent of the other institutions, of bodies and agencies and of the member states — independence is its defining legal feature. Seated in Frankfurt. Its tasks under Article 127 TFEU: to define and implement the Union's monetary policy, with PRICE STABILITY as the objective; to conduct foreign-exchange operations; to hold and manage the member states' official foreign reserves; and to promote the smooth operation of payment systems.

cards.q: What is the ECB's primary objective and where is it laid down?
cards.a: Price stability, in defining and implementing the Union's monetary policy under Article 127 TFEU. The ECB is independent of the institutions, bodies and member states.

slides.title: The European Court of Auditors
slides.text: Seated in Luxembourg, one member per member state. Under Article 287 TFEU it examines the accounts of all revenue and expenditure of the Union, including all bodies, offices and agencies. Three types of audit: FINANCIAL, whether the accounts accurately represent the financial situation; COMPLIANCE, whether transactions follow the rules; and PERFORMANCE, whether the funds achieve their goals efficiently. The third is the one that produces the politically uncomfortable reports.

cards.q: Name the three types of audit the European Court of Auditors carries out.
cards.a: Financial audits (do the accounts represent the true position), compliance audits (were the rules followed), and performance audits (are the funds achieving their goals efficiently).

slides.title: Four kinds of non-institutional actor
slides.text: Bodies, interinstitutional services, agencies, and interest groups — the four categories the rest of the lecture works through.

slides.title: Bodies: what they do
slides.text: Bodies help the Union perform its tasks, in two different ways. Some ADVISE the institutions — the European Economic and Social Committee, the European Committee of the Regions. Others ensure the institutions COMPLY with EU rules and procedures — the European Ombudsman, the European Data Protection Supervisor. The second group is a form of internal control that does not depend on litigation.

slides.title: The bodies, listed
slides.text: European External Action Service; European Economic and Social Committee; European Committee of the Regions; European Investment Bank; European Ombudsman; European Data Protection Supervisor; European Data Protection Board; European Public Prosecutor's Office; European Cybersecurity Competence Centre.

slides.title: The Committee of the Regions
slides.text: The voice of regions and cities: it advises on new laws affecting them, which is how the SUBSIDIARITY principle acquires an institutional guardian. Five-year terms, 350 members, who must be elected regional or local representatives, are proposed by member states and appointed by the Council, and must act independently in the Union's general interest. Its opinions are of three kinds: MANDATORY where an institution must request them, OPTIONAL where one may, and OWN-INITIATIVE where none was requested.

cards.q: Why is the Committee of the Regions linked to the subsidiarity principle?
cards.a: Because it advises on legislation affecting regions and cities, giving the level closest to citizens an institutional voice on whether the Union should act at all.

slides.title: The Economic and Social Committee
slides.text: An advisory body representing employers' and workers' organisations and other interest groups: five-year terms, 329 members from all member states, meeting nine times a year and acting independently of their governments. Opinions are adopted by simple majority and prepared by specialised sections and the consultative commission on industrial change; its observatories track EU strategies, and it maintains contact with national and regional economic and social councils.

slides.title: Interinstitutional services
slides.text: Shared infrastructure serving all the institutions, agencies and bodies — recruitment, staff development, IT and publishing. Four named: the Computer Emergency Response Team, the European School of Administration, the European Personnel Selection Office and the Publications Office.

slides.title: Two kinds of agency
slides.text: REGULATORY or decentralised agencies are established by legislative acts — by the legislature, with their own mandates. EXECUTIVE agencies are set up by the Commission on the basis of a general authorization from the Council and are an extension of the Commission. The difference matters for accountability: the first have their own legal personality and independence, the second do not.

cards.q: How does a decentralised EU agency differ from an executive agency?
cards.a: A decentralised (regulatory) agency is created by a legislative act, has its own legal personality and is independent, usually run by a management board. An executive agency is set up by the Commission under a Council authorization and is simply an extension of the Commission.

slides.title: Decentralised agencies in detail
slides.text: They have their own legal personality, are distinct from the institutions, are established under SECONDARY legislation, contribute to implementing EU policies, and are independent, usually governed by a management board. A Common Framework was agreed in 2012 between Parliament, Council and Commission. Their tasks are regulatory, operational and policy-related.

slides.title: Interest groups: who and how many
slides.text: EU-level associations, interest groups and NGOs; national associations, which are also assembled in the Economic and Social Committee; territorial associations of regions and cities, also organised in the Committee of the Regions; companies; and political, economic, technological and legal consultants. The scale: roughly 15,000 lobbyists and 2,600 interest organisations.

slides.title: Four roles of interest groups
slides.text: The slide sorts lobbying by the function it performs. As LOBBY, in the pluralist sense. As CONSULTANTS or experts, through open consultation during policy preparation and targeted consultation in working groups — the elite model. As CO-DECISION-MAKERS, through the Social Dialogue between trade unions and employers and through voluntary agreements concluded with the Commission. And as SUPERVISORY actors, through complaints, lawsuits and protest. The third category is the one that surprises: in EU social policy, the social partners can produce agreements that become law.

terms.def: Negotiation between EU-level trade union and employer organisations whose agreements can be implemented as Union law.

cards.q: In what sense can interest groups be co-decision-makers in the EU?
cards.a: Through the Social Dialogue, where agreements between EU-level trade unions and employers' organisations can be implemented as Union law, and through voluntary agreements concluded with the Commission.
